## Preparing the example data

SERRF normalisation requires complete (imputed), numeric feature data
with interspersed QC samples. Here we prepare `imputed_df` from
`example_metabolomics` by applying `filter_by_missingness()`,
`remove_outliers()`, `log1p()`, and `hybrid_imputation()`:

```{r setup}
library(OmicsProcessing)

data("example_metabolomics")
df <- example_metabolomics

filtered_df <- filter_by_missingness(
  df,
  row_thresh = 0.5,
  col_thresh = 0.5,
  target_cols = "@",
  is_qc = grepl("^sQC", df$sample_type),
  filter_order = "iterative"
)

clean_df <- remove_outliers(
  filtered_df,
  target_cols = "@",
  is_qc = grepl("^sQC", filtered_df$sample_type),
  method = "pca-lof-overall",
  impute_method = "half-min-value",
  restore_missing_values = TRUE,
  return_ggplots = FALSE
)$df_filtered

log_df <- clean_df %>%
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(tidyselect::contains("@"), log1p))

imputed_df <- hybrid_imputation(
  log_df,
  target_cols = "@",
  is_qc = grepl("^sQC", log_df$sample_type),
  method = "RF-LCMD",
  oobe_threshold = 0.1,
  control_RF = list(verbose = FALSE)
)$hybrid_rf_lcmd
```

## Batch correction using Systematical Error Removal using Random Forest (SERRF)

```{r serrf}
out_serrf <- normalise_SERRF(
  imputed_df,
  target_cols = "@",
  is_qc = grepl("^sQC", imputed_df$sample_type),
  strata_col = "batch"  # omit to treat all samples as one stratum
)
```

We can verify the reduction in technical variability by comparing the
standard deviation across pooled QC samples before and after SERRF
normalisation:

```{r serrf-check}
feature_cols <- resolve_target_cols(out_serrf, "@")
qc_rows <- grepl("^sQC", out_serrf$sample_type)

qc_sd_before <- apply(imputed_df[qc_rows, feature_cols], 2, sd)
qc_sd_after <- apply(out_serrf[qc_rows, feature_cols], 2, sd)

summary_df <- data.frame(
  median_qc_sd_before = round(median(qc_sd_before), 4),
  median_qc_sd_after = round(median(qc_sd_after), 4),
  pct_reduction = round(100 * (1 - median(qc_sd_after) / median(qc_sd_before)), 1)
)
summary_df
```

`normalise_SERRF()` models unwanted technical variation using
QC samples within each batch/stratum and applies SERRF normalisation to
the specified feature columns. Use `target_cols` to select features by
name or regular expression (resolved via `resolve_target_cols()`), and
supply a logical `is_qc` flag for each row. See the reference:
[`normalise_SERRF()`](../reference/normalise_SERRF.html).

### Input requirements

- `strata_col`: provide the batch/strata column when it exists; if you
  omit it, a dummy single-level stratum is created so all samples are
  treated as one batch. If supplied, it is coerced to a factor (no NAs).
- `is_qc` is a logical vector the same length as `nrow(df)`; ensure
  every batch has enough QC samples for the SERRF model.
- All `target_cols` must be numeric and **contain no NA values** (impute
  beforehand).
- Ensure the number of target features exceeds `num_screen_SERRF`
  (default `10`), or lower `num_screen_SERRF` accordingly when testing on
  a small feature subset.

### Tuning and tips

- `num_screen_SERRF` (default `10`) controls how many correlated features
  are screened per target; increase cautiously if you have many features
  and stable QC coverage.
- Inspect before/after QC variability or run-order plots with
  [`plot_omics_distributions()`](plot-omics-distributions.html) to verify
  that batch drift is reduced.
- Keep batches balanced: very small batches or few QC points can lead to
  unstable fits; consider merging sparse strata or adding QC if
  possible.
